items.prompt: What is a crocodile farm or alligator farm?

options.label: An establishment for breeding and raising crocodilians to produce meat, leather, and other goods.
options.feedback: Correct. That is exactly what the farm does.

options.label: A place where crocodilians are only kept for tourists to see.
options.feedback: Some early farms were only tourist attractions, but the definition of a farm is about breeding for products.

options.label: A sanctuary where wild crocodilians are protected from hunters.
options.feedback: Farms are for producing goods, not primarily for protection.

options.label: A laboratory where crocodilians are studied by scientists.
options.feedback: Farms are for production, not scientific research.

items.ok_line: A crocodile farm breeds and raises crocodilians for their meat and skin.
items.ko_line: A farm produces goods, not just shows animals.
items.exp_text: A crocodile farm or alligator farm is an establishment for breeding and raising crocodilians to produce meat, leather from their skin, and other goods. Many species are farmed internationally.

items.prompt: Which of these is one of the three ways to obtain crocodilians recognized by CITES and the Crocodile Specialist Group?

options.label: Poaching from the wild
options.feedback: Poaching is illegal hunting, not one of the recognized ways. The three ways are ranching, wild harvesting, and captive breeding.

options.label: Ranching
options.feedback: Correct. Ranching is one of the three recognized ways to obtain crocodilians, along with wild harvesting and captive breeding.

options.label: Tourism
options.feedback: Tourism is an additional source of revenue for some facilities, but it is not a way to obtain crocodilians.

options.label: Disease control
options.feedback: Disease control is a welfare concern, not a method of obtaining animals.

items.ok_line: Ranching, wild harvesting, and captive breeding are recognized ways.
items.ko_line: Tourism and poaching are not among the three recognized methods.
items.exp_text: The three ways to obtain crocodilians recognized by CITES and the Crocodile Specialist Group are ranching, wild harvesting, and captive breeding.

items.prompt: What is the main difference between an alligator farm and an alligator ranch?

options.label: A farm breeds alligators on site, while a ranch only incubates and raises hatchlings collected from the wild.
options.feedback: Correct. Farms keep breeding adults to produce their own eggs, whereas ranches collect eggs from the wild and do not breed adults.

options.label: A farm only collects eggs from the wild, while a ranch breeds alligators on site.
options.feedback: That is the opposite. Ranches collect from the wild; farms breed their own.

options.label: A farm is for tourism, while a ranch is for meat production.
options.feedback: Both farms and ranches can produce meat and leather; the difference is in how they obtain the animals.

options.label: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable.
options.feedback: They are not the same. Farms breed adults, ranches do not.

items.ok_line: Farms breed adults; ranches incubate wild-collected eggs.
items.ko_line: The key is whether breeding adults are kept on site.
items.exp_text: Alligator farms breed alligators, keeping breeding adults in their facilities to produce eggs. Ranches do not keep breeding adults; they incubate and rear hatchlings collected from the wild.

items.prompt: What does an 'open cycle' operation aim to do?

options.label: Harvest as many crocodilians as possible for profit.
options.feedback: That describes a closed-cycle operation, which is primarily concerned with harvest, not conservation.

options.label: Keep adult females in captivity to produce eggs for harvest.
options.feedback: That is part of a closed-cycle operation, not an open cycle.

options.label: Protect the wild population but also earn profit from meat.
options.feedback: An open cycle focuses on the health of the wild population, not on profit from harvest.

options.label: Support the health of the wild population by using captive rearing to supplement it.
options.feedback: Correct. Open cycle programs use captive rearing to help the wild population, not to harvest for profit.

items.ok_line: Open cycle aims to support wild populations.
items.ko_line: Closed cycle focuses on harvest, not conservation.
items.exp_text: Open cycle programs are concerned with the health of the wild population and use captive rearing to supplement the wild numbers. They are not focused on economic profit.

items.prompt: What disease causes a brown residue to form around the eyes, oral cavity, and tail of hatchling and juvenile crocodilians?

options.label: Crocodile pox
options.feedback: Correct. Crocodile pox, caused by Parapoxvirus, causes a brown residue around the eyes, oral cavity, and tail.

options.label: Caiman pox
options.feedback: Caiman pox causes white lesions, not a brown residue.

options.label: Adenoviral hepatitis
options.feedback: Adenoviral hepatitis causes organ failure and death, not a brown residue.

options.label: Mycoplasmosis
options.feedback: Mycoplasmosis causes polyarthritis and pneumonia, not a brown residue.

items.ok_line: Crocodile pox leaves a brown residue on young animals.
items.ko_line: Caiman pox leaves white lesions, not brown.
items.exp_text: Crocodile pox is caused by Parapoxvirus and affects hatchlings and juveniles. It causes a brown residue to form around the eyes, oral cavity, and tail.

items.prompt: What are the three ways to obtain crocodilians recognized by CITES and the Crocodile Specialist Group?

options.label: Hunting, trapping, and fishing
options.feedback: Hunting, trapping, and fishing are methods for taking wild animals, but they are not the three recognized ways for obtaining crocodilians. The recognized ways are ranching, wild harvesting, and captive breeding.

options.label: Farming, poaching, and tourism
options.feedback: Poaching is illegal and not a recognized method, and tourism is a way facilities earn extra money, not a way to obtain crocodilians. The correct recognized categories are ranching, wild harvesting, and captive breeding.

options.label: Ranching, wild harvesting, and captive breeding
options.feedback: That's correct. These three categories are the ways recognized by CITES and the Crocodile Specialist Group for obtaining crocodilians.

options.label: Egg collection, juvenile release, and skinning
options.feedback: Egg collection and skinning are steps within farming or ranching, and juvenile release is a conservation action, but none of these are the recognized categories for obtaining crocodilians. The correct ones are ranching, wild harvesting, and captive breeding.

items.ok_line: Ranching, wild harvesting, and captive breeding are the official ways.
items.ko_line: Those are not the three categories CITES and the CSG use.
items.exp_text: The three ways to obtain crocodilians are ranching, wild harvesting, and captive breeding. Ranching means incubating and rearing hatchlings collected from the wild, while captive breeding keeps adult breeders to produce eggs on site, and wild harvesting refers to taking eggs or animals from nature.

items.prompt: What does an open-cycle crocodilian operation focus on?

options.label: Harvesting as many animals as possible
options.feedback: That describes a closed-cycle operation, which is primarily concerned with harvest. An open-cycle operation is concerned with the health of the wild population, not just maximizing harvest.

options.label: Keeping all adult females in captivity
options.feedback: That is a feature of closed-cycle operations, where adult females are kept in captivity to lay eggs for harvest. Open-cycle operations focus on supporting wild populations.

options.label: Making the highest profit for the owners
options.feedback: Profit is the main concern of closed-cycle operations, not open-cycle ones. Open-cycle operations aim for the overall health of the species, even though costs may be similar.

options.label: The health of the wild population
options.feedback: Correct. Open-cycle programs use captive rearing to supplement wild populations, so their main goal is the well-being of the species in the wild.

items.ok_line: It aims for the health of the wild population.
items.ko_line: Profit and harvest belong to closed-cycle operations.
items.exp_text: Open-cycle operations are concerned with the health of the wild population. They use captive rearing as a way to supplement or support wild numbers, rather than aiming primarily at harvest or profit.

items.prompt: Which disease is caused by a Parapoxvirus and affects hatchlings and juveniles?

options.label: Caiman pox
options.feedback: Caiman pox is caused by a different virus and causes white lesions, but the disease caused by Parapoxvirus is crocodile pox, and it causes a brown residue.

options.label: Crocodile pox
options.feedback: Correct. Crocodile pox is caused by Parapoxvirus and affects hatchlings and juveniles, causing a brown residue around the eyes, oral cavity, and tail.

options.label: Mycoplasmosis
options.feedback: Mycoplasmosis causes polyarthritis and pneumonia, not a skin disease with a brown residue. It is not caused by Parapoxvirus.

options.label: Adenoviral hepatitis
options.feedback: Adenoviral hepatitis causes organ failure and death, not the skin residue seen in crocodile pox. It is not caused by Parapoxvirus.

items.ok_line: Parapoxvirus causes crocodile pox in young crocodilians.
items.ko_line: The virus and symptoms point only to crocodile pox.
items.exp_text: Crocodile pox is caused by Parapoxvirus and affects hatchlings and juveniles. It produces a brown residue around the eyes, oral cavity, and tail. Caiman pox, in contrast, is a separate disease with white lesions.
